::: {.callout-note title="Overview"}
This week we focus on two strands of learning:

A.  The linear model

So far, we've looked at measures of association between two variables using correlation. **This week you will learn about regression and the linear model as a way of predicting one variable from knowledge of one or more other variables.**

When considering one predictor, regression tells us a lot of the same things as correlation does. Regression becomes really useful when we have more than one predictor. We will talk about that in weeks 8 and 9. We will do all this in the context of the **Clearly Understood** project on how easy or difficult people find it to understand written health information.

B.  Research project: Build the questionnaire study on Gorilla

We will also continue the group project by focussing on building the study on Gorilla, ready for data collection next week.

The materials we have prepared to support your learning are arranged in
four parts:

-   Lectures
-   Reading
-   Pre-lab activities
-   Lab activities

You can navigate to each in the side bar on the right
:::

## Lectures {#sec-4141-w7-lectures}

::: callout-note
Please note that Rob may mention a different module code or different week during the lectures. I've reviewed the material and the content is highly relevant to the current module.
:::

::: callout-tip
In week 7, we aim to further develop skills in *analysing* and in *visualising* psychological data. We will do so in the context of the **Clearly Understood** project.

We will aim to answer the research question: What person attributes in adult readers predict success in understanding written health information?

Research questions like this can be examined **using linear models**.

When we do these analyses, we will need to think about how we report the results and decide:

- is the association significant?
- does the association reflect a positive or negative relationship between outcome and predictor?
- is the association relatively strong or weak?

Our thinking, and our decision-making, will be helped by developing our data visualisation skills.
At every stage, as we work, we will visualize the data to understand the shape of the relationships we may observe or predict.
:::

### Lab activity 3: Reminders through association

For this lab, we're going to use data from [**Rogers, T. & Milkman, K.
L. (2016). Reminders through association. *Psychological Science, 27*,
973-986.**](https://journals.sagepub.com/stoken/default+domain/6XgDSfr6ZHSDs47tx5bu/full)
You can read the full paper online but the short version is that the
authors looked at how people remember to follow through with the
intention of doing something.

Although there are lots of potential reasons (e.g., some people may lack
the self-control resources), Rogers and Milkman (2016) propose that some
people fail to follow through simply because they forget about their
good intentions. If this is the case, the authors argue, then having
visual reminders to follow through on their intentions may help people
remember to keep them. For example, a person may choose to put a sticker
for their gym on their car window, so that every time they get in the
car they remember to go to the gym.

In Study 1 by Rogers and colleagues, participants took part in an
unrelated experiment but at the start of the task they were asked to
return a small stack of paper clips to the reception of the building at
the end of the study and if they did so the researchers would donate \$1
to a charity. They were then asked if they intended to do this. Those in
the reminder-through-association (RTA) condition read "Thank you! To
remind you to pick up a paper clip, an elephant statuette will be
sitting on the counter as you collect your payment." This message was
followed by a picture of the elephant statuette. Those in the control
condition simply read "Thank you!".

What we want to do is to run a chi-square analysis to determine whether
those in the reminder-through-association condition were more likely to
remember to return the paper-clips than those in the control condition.

#### Aims of the activity

We are going to:

1.  Setup the appropriate bits and pieces in RStudio
2.  Read in the data files
3.  Do some data wrangling using `filter()`
4.  Do some more data wrangling using `mutate()` and `recode_values()`
5.  Extract descriptive statistics
6.  Visualise the data with a bar chart
7.  Run the chi-square analysis
8.  Check the assumptions
9.  Calculate the effect size
10. Check the adjusted standardised residuals
11. Write up the results

#### Step 3: Some data wrangling - Use `filter()` to keep relevant data

We need to do a little bit of wrangling to get our data into the format
we need: First, we need to remove all the participants who said that
they did not intend to return the paper-clips (intend = 0) as we are
only interested in whether people follow through on an intention.

> Action: Insert a new code chunk and use `filter()` to remove all
> participants who said that they did not intend to return the
> paper-clips. Can a look below for a reminder on how `filter()` works.
> Give it a go. If you're stuck, have a look at the Code below.

::: {.callout-tip title="How does `filter()` work?"}
The `filter()` function allows you to select specific rows from a data
frame based on one or more conditions.

For example, imagine we have a dataset containing information about
participants in a psychology study, including their age and gender. We
might want to select only participants who are over 18 years old.

We can do this using:

``` r
filter(data, age > 18)
```

Here: - `data` is the name of our data frame. - `age > 18` is the
condition we want to apply. - note these two bits of information are
separated within the function by a comma. - only rows where the
condition is `TRUE` are kept.

We can also apply multiple conditions. For example, to select
participants who are over 18 **and** identify as a woman:

``` r
filter(data, age > 18, gender == "Woman")
```

When we provide multiple conditions separated by commas, `filter()`
keeps only rows that satisfy **all** of the conditions.

Some useful operators for filtering data include:

| Operator | Meaning                  | Example             |
|----------|--------------------------|---------------------|
| `==`     | Equal to                 | `gender == "Woman"` |
| `!=`     | Not equal to             | `gender != "Woman"` |
| `>`      | Greater than             | `age > 18`          |
| `<`      | Less than                | `age < 30`          |
| `>=`     | Greater than or equal to | `age >= 18`         |
| `<=`     | Less than or equal to    | `age <= 30`         |

We can also use `&` (AND) and `|` (OR) to combine conditions.

For example:

``` r
filter(data, age >= 18 & age <= 30)
```

This selects participants aged between 18 and 30 (inclusive).
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Code" collapse="true"}
``` r
intent_data <- filter(intent_data, intend == 1)
```
:::

**Question Step 3**

a.  How many participants were removed because they didn't intend to
    return the paper-clips?

#### Step 4: Some more data wrangling - Use `recode_values()` to have text labels

To make the output easier to read, we’re going to recode the values for
our key variables (`condition` and `actualdonate`) to have text labels
rather than numerical values.

For this we can use the functions `mutate()` and `recode_values()`.

> Action: Insert a new code chunk and use `mutate()` and
> `recode_values()` to change the numerical values for `condition` and
> `actualdonate` to text labels. The code to do this is below. You can
> copy it, but have a good look to make sure you understand what each
> bit does.

``` r
intent_data = mutate(
  intent_data,
  condition = recode_values(condition, 1 ~ "rta", 2 ~ "control"),
  actualdonate = recode_values(actualdonate, 1 ~ "donated", 0 ~ "no_donation"))
```

::: callout-tip
Have a look at the recipe for `mutate()` for more information on this
function [here](https://posit.cloud/learn/recipes/transform/TransformF).
:::

#### Step 5: Descriptive statistics

Next you need to calculate descriptive statistics. For frequency data
these are simply counts so we can use the function `count()` to do this.
We want to know how many participants are in each group (rta - donated,
rta - didn’t donate, control - donated, control - didn’t donate).

> Action: Insert a new code chunk and use `count()` to check how many
> participants are in each group (rta - donated, rta - didn’t donate,
> control - donated, control - didn’t donate). You may also want to
> calculate the percentages of participants in each condition. The code
> to do this is below. You can copy it, but have a good look to make
> sure you understand what each bit does.

``` r
intent_counts <- mutate(
  count(intent_data, condition, actualdonate),
  percent = 100 * n / sum(n),
  .by = condition)
intent_counts
```

**Questions Step 5**

a.  How many participants in the control condition didn’t donate?
b.  How many participants in the control condition donated?
c.  How many participants in the RTA condition didn’t donate?
d.  How many participants in the rta condition donated?

#### Step 6: Data visualisation using `geom_bar()`

We want to create a simple bar plot of our count data. We'll use
`ggplot()` for this in combination with the `geom_bar()` function.

> Action: Insert a new code chunk and use the code template below to
> create a bar chart. Make sure to fill in the relevant bits.

``` r
ggplot(data = , aes(x = , fill = )) +
  geom_bar(position = "dodge")
```

::: {.callout-note title="Code" collapse="true"}
The code to do this is below:

```         
ggplot(data = intent_data, aes(x = condition, fill = actualdonate)) +
  geom_bar(position = "dodge")
```
:::

**Questions Step 6**

a.  What does `position = "dodge"` do? Remove it and rerun the code to
    find out.
b.  Describe the pattern in the data in your own words.

As you can see, the plot makes it much easier to get your head around
what the data mean: Participants in the RTA condition appear to have
been more likely to remember to donate than those in the control
condition.

The `ggplot2()` package allows you to customise all aspects of your
plots, so let’s tidy ours up a little bit. We’re going to do the
following:

-   Edit the labels on the x-axis, y-axis and fill
-   Change the colours of the bars by using `scale_fill_manual()` and
    specifying the colours we want in the values argument
-   Change the theme of the plot to change how it looks

> Action: Copy the code below to a new code chunk. In your Quarto
> document, write a comment to describe what each line of code does.

``` r
ggplot(data = intent_data, aes(x = condition, fill = actualdonate)) +
  geom_bar(position = "dodge") +
  scale_x_discrete(name = "Condition", labels = c("Control", "RTA")) +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Count") +
  scale_fill_manual(name = "Behaviour", labels = c("Donated", "Did not donate"), values = c("blue", "grey"))+
  theme_classic()
```

There are a few things to note about the code we just added on:

-   If you use simple colour names then you are restricted in the
    options you can choose, however, if you want more flexibility you
    can use hexadecimal colour codes, see
    [**here**](http://www.cookbook-r.com/Graphs/Colors_(ggplot2)/).
-   There are multiple themes that you can apply. Have a look at the
    `ggplot2()` cheatsheet for an overview
    ([**here**](https://rstudio.github.io/cheatsheets/html/data-visualization.html?_gl=1*7olq9v*_ga*MjEyNjQ2Nzk4MC4xNzA1NTg2MzI1*_ga_2C0WZ1JHG0*MTcwNjM1OTgzMi4xNC4xLjE3MDYzNjA1MjUuMC4wLjA.#themes)).
    Try out a few and see which one you prefer.

#### Step 7: Run the chi-square analysis

Now let's run that chi-square analysis to see whether our impression
from the plot holds up and there is a significant association between
the grouping variables.

> Action: Copy the code snippet below to a new code chunk.

``` r
results <- chisq.test(x = intent_data$condition,
y = intent_data$actualdonate,
correct = FALSE)
results
```

::: {.callout-note title="How does `chisq.test()` work?"}
```         
results <- chisq.test(x = intent_recode$condition,        # the first grouping variable
                      y = intent_recode$actualdonate,     # the second grouping variable
                      correct = FALSE)                    # whether we want to apply the continuity correction (use if any of the expected cell frequencies < 10 in 2 x 2 table)
results
```
:::

**Question Step 7:** What do you conclude from the output?

#### Step 8: Check the assumptions

The assumptions for chi-square are as follows:

1)  The data in the cells should be frequencies, or counts of cases
    rather than percentages.
2)  The levels (or categories) of the variables are mutually exclusive.
    That is, a particular participant fits into one and only one group
    of each of the variables.
3)  Each participant may contribute data to one and only one cell. If,
    for example, the same participants are tested over time such that
    the comparisons are of the same subjects at Time 1, Time 2, Time 3,
    etc., then Chi-square may not be used.
4)  The study groups must be independent. This means that a different
    test must be used if the two groups are related. For example, a
    different test must be used if the researcher’s data consists of
    paired samples, such as in studies in which a parent is paired with
    his or her child.
5)  There are 2 variables, and both are measured as categories, usually
    at the nominal level. While Chi-square has no rule about limiting
    the number of cells (by limiting the number of categories for each
    variable), a very large number of cells (over 20) can make it
    difficult to meet assumption #6 below, and to interpret the meaning
    of the results.
6)  The expected cell frequencies should be greater than 5.

Assumptions 1) to 5) should be evaluated by reviewing the design of the
study. The only assumption that we need to check with R is whether all
expected frequencies are greater than 5. This information is in the
object in which you stored the results of the Chi-square test, under
`expected`.

> Action: Copy the code snippet below to a new code chunk.

``` r
results$expected
```

**Question Step 8:** What do you conclude from the output?

#### Step 9: Calculate the effect size

The last step before writing up the results is to calculate an effect
size so that we have a standardised measure of how large the association
between our grouping variables is. The effect size measure for
chi-square is Cramer’s V. To calculate Cramer’s V we’re going to use the
function `cramers_v()` from the `easystats` package. The code mirrors
the code used for the Chi-square test itself.

> Action: Copy the code snippet below to a new code chunk.

``` r
effect_size <- cramers_v(x = intent_data$condition,     
                         y = intent_data$actualdonate) 
effect_size
```

We can square the effect size (or multiple it by itself) to see how much
variance in one variable is accounted for by the other variable. Use the
code snippet below to square the effect size.

``` r
percentageAccountedFor <- effect_size * effect_size *100
percentageAccountedFor
```

**Question Step 9:** How large is the effect and how much variance is
accounted for?

#### Step 10: Adjusted standardised residuals

To help interpret the relationship, it is useful to look at the adjusted
standardised residuals. These are z-scores showing how many standard
deviations each observed count is above or below the count expected if
the variables were unrelated, so they indicate which cells differ most
from expectation. Because they approximately follow a standard normal
distribution, values beyond ±1.96 indicate a difference at *p* \< .05
(two-tailed), beyond ±2.58 at *p* \< .01, and beyond ±3.29 at *p* \<
.001.

> Action: Copy the code snippet below to a new code chunk.

``` r
results$residuals   # check the adjusted standardised residuals
```

**Question Step 10:** What do you conclude from the output?

#### Step 11: Write up the results following APA guidelines.

Using the guidance below, have a go at writing up the results for the
Chi-square analysis following APA guidelines.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
The [**Purdue writing lab
website**](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/research_and_citation/apa_style/apa_formatting_and_style_guide/apa_numbers_statistics.html)
is helpful for guidance on punctuating statistics.
:::
